utterances.text: So this picture is in the direction looking east, so the enclave is at the left of the picture. And this aerial photograph spots, in fact, the location where the six secondary graves are located.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And how did you find those secondary graves?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Initially we had a human source that enabled us to spot two of these sites. And subsequently having checked that indeed there were multiple remains in them, we insisted on additional searches for aerial imagery. And this is how we came up with imagery analysis that enabled to find six of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go to 254.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is, we call them Zeleni Jadar because it's the name of the area. This is the secondary grave number 4, so ZJ-4. And that was our first check of just underneath the surface. And here appears a human body.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: 255. Another illustration?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm. So we are now in the secondary phase of the burial process. This is a group of graves, secondary graves, along the former road that went from Zvornik to Tuzla which is now a totally more or less abandoned road. And this is a location close to Orahovac. The result of the exhumation of those sites, I mean, not all of them, but several of them, indicates that the bodies were coming, indeed, from Orahovac. This was the secondary burial place for the bodies that had been taken away from the two graves of Orahovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And how did -- how were those graves found?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: These ones, like all of the other ones we are talking about, were found based on aerial imagery analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. 256.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is, again, the so-called Hodzici Road with the aerial photograph that shows the dispersion of these secondary sites all along this stretch of dirt road.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did you go yourself to any of these sites to determine if there were any human remains there before the full exhumations?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely, yes, I went to all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what -- did you confirm anything?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: On some, no confirmation; but on others, yes, there was confirmation. But, nevertheless, all of them were put on the list for full exhumation. I don't know if at this stage it's still done, because we abandoned this exhumation aspect in 2001 to the Bosniaks and it turned -- becoming an extremely slow process after 2001.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And that will be the subject of an additional report, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, let's go to 257.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is another cluster of graves in a -- secondary graves in the area we name Liplje. And, again, the Djakovica location indicated that, yes, there were multiple remains, so potentially mass graves. And after exhumation, the connection was made by the analysts of the evidence found inside as bodies coming from the dam, from Petkovci; Petkovci school, exhumation of the dam.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just for the Trial Chamber, do you recall any examples of how the connections were made, what kind of materials were related to both places?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The main connection for all of them was shell casings analysis, since the shell casings were scattered all over the dead bodies, all over the crime scene. Then these shell casings for many of them were buried together with the bodies. And when these shell casings -- when the bodies were taken out of these graves to be put in secondary graves, again the shell casings were found. So there was a full analysis process of all the shell casings to make matches between sites. But in addition to the shell casings, there were also additional elements: soil analysis; pollen analysis; green glass, for example, found in a place we have not hit yet but coming obviously from Kozluk, with the labels. The piece of severed pipe that was torn apart at Orahovac was found in a grave at Hodzici. Pieces of the concrete structure of the Kravica warehouse was found in one of the graves of Glogova. So, I mean, there is full testimony getting into the detail of all the findings that connect the places each with another.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. I think we now should go to 258.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: So this is the area of Liplje where these four graves, secondary graves, of those executed at the plateau of the dam were then hidden.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. 259.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is what we name the Cancari Road, which is a dirt road in a valley. And these first nine spots indicate the location of secondary graves which the forensic experts could connect with the bodies taken away from the Branjevo farm.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Any Kozluk connection that you remember?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It will come on the following slide where three more dots have to be added on this valley.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's keep going then. We should be on 260.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the view of the how looks the Cancari valley. It's a remote place that has been totally ravaged by -- during the war time. All the houses are destroyed. And makes a perfect hiding place for this type of secondary graves.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And 261.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: So this is a full view of aerial imagery showing the entire Cancari valley. The nine sites connected with Branjevo farm are at the left of the pictures, so at the west. And there are three more sites that appear in this red box. So in total 12 sites in the valley. The first three being, in fact, the bodies that have been taken out from the mass grave of Kozluk. And it's in one of these that when we saw the labels Vitinka and the green glass we could instantly, indeed, make a connection.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to 262.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: So this is a picture taken from the aerial imagery in order to put it in a shape. This is seen from far above. And the next one will be a view from a helicopter.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: So this is how a secondary grave looks, and this is the set-up of a -- for the exhumation team, which is going to go entirely through this site which is the first one we processed in the valley, Cancari 12.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did you make a video for courtroom presentation to show, give the Trial Chamber some -- a more specific detailed idea of a secondary grave exhumation?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. The purpose of that initially was not to be used in the courtroom, but I did it in order to show for the newcomers of the exhumation team who are archaeologists what it is to -- what they are going to do, since these bones were not a few thousands years old, it was a bit of a new business for them also.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. One more photograph, 264. What's this?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the first layer after the start of the exhumation of Cancari 12.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you just give us a brief explanation how they got to be in this sort of odd position like this with trenches on either side?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The experts will better talk about it than I would do, but the problem they face in these situations is that these bodies have been first buried with heavy equipment, after that they have been unburied with heavy equipment, put on board of trucks, then re-dumped in secondary graves; so many of them are body parts because they have been sliced by the spoon of these heavy machines, and all the bodies are a bit more or less intertwined. So for the sake of their work to take the body parts as undamaged as possible, it was a very, very difficult task for them to work on these secondary sites.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we now have 19 minutes. It's really the only video evidence of this massive exhumation project. So I would play this 19-minute tape. It's our number 1306.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And if you can provide any necessary narrative.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: So that's the arrival on Cancari 12. So from the ground it's more or less impossible to see that something has been disturbed here. When you are at the level of the ground, you don't see it. You have to look at it from above. So that's a 360 of the area. Only destroyed houses. The road that, to the left, goes to the Drina valley, about 8 kilometres from here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: During the exhumation, do you recall any Dutch jeeps driving up and down the road?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not a Dutch jeep, it was a jeep from the police that had been stolen to the Dutch battalion during the take-over of Srebrenica. So here they are, in fact, mapping entirely the terrain. Taking reference points. Then the little backhoe will start to take action and scoop -- scoop a first layer of the terrain in order to determine what is the real surface of the grave.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Who is the man in the hat?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Richard -- Professor Richard Wright, who is overlooking the operation. Now he is marking the terrain due to, in fact, difference of colours of the soil. The earth turns green on such burial places because of the melting of the bodies with the soil. It becomes greenish. By putting these little markers, he is finding the limits of the grave. So we were a little bit off limits because digging what was supposed to be just after the limit, there were remains.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Flags were supposed to fix the limits of the grave so the backhoe, after this limit, could dig. But unfortunately the limit was a bit too short apparently, and when the backhoe dug, he ended up hitting human remains.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Is that the correct date of this?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: For sure, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: November 5th, 1998. Excuse me, 11 May 1998.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is a trench dug alongside of the graves so that they can work through the grave. But on this specific site we requested also that they work first the surface so we could visualise the surface.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: These people we see now, do you know -- were they professionals or are they just labourers?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they are all very highly qualified in their activity. They are all archaeologists coming from various countries. So this is a hand. When we first came on this site, the first dig revealed the presence of a human foot, and we will see this foot now fully exhumed soon. There is also a search for shell casings on-going during the exhumation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's -- is that what the -- that's a metal detector?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely, yes. This is a skull. That's the beep indicating the metal detector had found a shell casing. Here it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you recall this Cancari 12 particular -- do you know what site you think this was connected to?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Branjevo farm. So you can see it's like an archeological dig. This is why the process is so lengthy also, but very precise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: In your time, were they ever able to figure out how many people this represents?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I recall is that most of these sites -- I know that one at least is much larger but was exhumed after my departure. Most of them were between 80 and 180 people inside. So every evening the team was covering the site to protect it in case it will rain. The place was guarded day and night.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How about any de-mining?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, when the exhumation team arrived on the spot, there was previous de-mining. What we did not do when we were doing the first assessment of it, it would have taken much too much time. This is the foot that we found when we went to this place the first time, because there was a preliminary dig on all these sites prior deciding to start the exhumation. So every one of them, remains, were found.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you personally use a shovel to find many of these sites?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. That's a view from above.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you briefly tell us where they are taking these human remains?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: At this point, they are taken to a container. And then later on they are taken to the morgue. And at the morgue every body or piece of body is being autopsied.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And in your time was that done by an international team from the OTP?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. Yes, yes. It started in 1996 and it didn't stop. This is an example of the difficulties they face in order to get out a body part intertwined with other body parts. Sometimes to take only one leg out of it can take a lot of time. And I cannot avoid to make always the same comment when we hit these pictures is that the thing that is missing on them is the smell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Ruez, just the last few photographs in your book. I will go now to 268. We've gone over these -- each of these graves, so I'll go over to page 268 now.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The map before would be worth returning to, the one just before this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right, team leader, let's go back. This is page 267.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Now, this one is of interest because, again, it's just a graphic thing, but this marks all the most important crime scenes of this case. The primary burial sites which are undisturbed, so just the few ones at the south. All the main ones are totally disturbed. And the locations of the secondary ones will be needed to have all the crime scenes, all the concentration sites of prisoners. It will add too many items on the map, but this shows the scale of this operation, both in the distance but also in the number of sites involved. And it's a crime scene that is 70 kilometres north/south and 40 kilometres east/west. So it's not the usual scale of a traditional crime scene.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And the people that helped exhume that, Bill Haglund, Richard Wright, where did they get their experience, just very briefly, so we know. Just -- Bill Haglund, for example?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bill Haglund, prior working for this case, did exhumations in Rwanda. Richard Wright did exhumation in Ukraine on war crimes from the Second World War.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. All right. I think we can now go to 268.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: So this is a picture that I could assemble thanks again to the video of Zoran Petrovic when he went to Srebrenica town. And this is the last picture of the standing mosque in the centre of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And do you remember what date Petrovic would have gone into Srebrenica to take this photograph?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could be the 13.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Let's go now to 269.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the same mosque but after the take-over of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And who took this picture?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I took this picture.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Would you remember roughly when?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1996. Probably around April, April or May.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go to 270.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's at least one year later, as seen from above. That was probably 1997. You can still see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can we put that on e-court so he can ... It's a bit hard to make out, I think, where this is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could you just circle the area that you are talking about?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'd like to offer that into evidence as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to 271.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P92, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This is 271.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's a closer shot of the previous one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. I think that's clear. Now, let's go to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, we saw a lengthy video of the exhumation, do you want --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I apologise. Yes. I now -- that is number 1306. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P93, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So I think we see where you were talking about. As you said, it's an enlargement. So if we could go now to the next shot, which is 272. What's this?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: So this is, again, one year later again, but this time there is nothing left to be seen because it has been levelled to the ground and now it's -- where the yellow arrow points, it's just part of the parking-lot of this area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. We also see a structure with a tower or steeple; what is that?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an Orthodox church that is still intact, at least the outside, as one can see, at that date.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go to 273.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's another mosque in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And 274.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's another view of the minaret.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Same thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what happened to that particular mosque?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't follow this one as closely as the other one, so I cannot say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And the last picture in your book. This, again, we see is a shot of what town?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bratunac town.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And this time we clearly see a picture of the -- down on the right-hand corner, of the Bratunac Brigade; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. As well as the other things that you've mentioned before.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: And this one should fit in the part that we dedicated to Bratunac being at the evening of 13 of July, the main assembling area for all of the prisoners taken during the operation, I mean, taken between the 12 and the 13 evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, Mr. President -- Thank you, Mr. Ruez. -- that brings this -- his testimony, from the Prosecution's perspective, to a close. I would offer this book into evidence, the electronic version, as well as the hard copy, 1450.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This compilation of photos and the book will be received.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we have hard copies of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P94, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We have hard copies of this, if the Court wishes to have them. Otherwise, I guess it's break time as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The Chamber will appreciate to receive that, the hard copy. And I think now we adjourn for the second break. And then, Mr. Tolimir, you can start cross-examination. We adjourn and resume at 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, please start your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. My greetings to all those present. May peace be with you, and may this trial be completed in accordance with God's will. I would like to thank the Prosecution, specifically Mr. McCloskey, for having presented some elements from the investigation that may be helpful to the Defence, since the Defence did not have an opportunity to conduct this sort of investigation out in the field and is unable to hear out the eye-witnesses of these events as Mr. Ruez could have for a period of time while he was the OTP investigator. And I would like to thank Mr. Ruez for providing me with certain elements in replying to the questions put by the Prosecution which will help shed light on certain facts. And I'm sure that through the examination, Mr. Ruez will be able to provide certain helpful information that will be of assistance to the Trial Chamber as well in establishing matters related to had case. I would like to commence my examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Depending on how cross-examination will develop, we will be drawing upon some of the comments that you made which were very extensive, and at some points you also drew certain conclusions. The Defence believes that based on the elements presented by you in the examination-in-chief will require ten hours to complete their examination, which is the amount of time used up by the Prosecution. And, at any rate, the Prosecution will have an opportunity to re-examine you. Before I proceed to ask you about your personal background, I would like to put to you several general questions related to the book that you presented over the two days now, and which was also presented in the Popovic et al. case. And I hope we shall be able to complete these questions today, otherwise it will take us to April. It's, in fact, a series of photographs that I would like you to answer certain questions about. Based on which criteria did you select the photographs that you included in your book?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed, these pictures are an extract of a much larger set of pictures. The selection is done in the purpose to be as short and precise as possible for a short presentation of this long series of events, and enable people who have no opportunity to go and see these places by themselves to have a feeling of how they look like or how they looked like.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us when the book was made. Was it during your term of office as the chief investigator of the ICTY for Srebrenica, or thereafter? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: In fact, this book exists now in the format of a book, but for me it was a bit like a PowerPoint presentation. It was -- always was an electronic version, and it improved, let's say, with time, because I used more or less the same exhibits for all the trials I testified for. So this specific one was indeed done just -- finalised just before the trial you mentioned; Popovic, Beara, and others, the seven.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. We can, therefore, conclude that you did the work for the purposes of your testimony in that case? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ruez, yesterday during your testimony at page 6 of the transcript, you gave us comments on a map.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we call up Prosecution 65 ter 01450, page 5. Do we have it? Thank you, we have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You said that the grey line roughly depicted the boundaries of Srebrenica, that's to say, the Srebrenica enclave, because, and I quote: "There was no actual boundary, and that's the boundary of the protected area." What is it exactly that you meant, and what's the basis for your conclusion as presented to the Trial Chamber? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The reason why I didn't name the grey line boundary is because according to what I heard both from the Bosniaks who were inside, from people from the UN Battalion who was there, and also from Bosnian Serb army personnel was that this could not be called boundaries. It was -- it was lines which were, in fact, moving with the time. When UN soldiers were leaving an area, sometimes then it was chewed up by the Bosnian Serb army. So these lines, in fact, only exist through the position of the observation posts. It was not something frozen on a map.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. For Their Honours' benefit, can you tell us, since you were involved in the investigation concerning Srebrenica, do you know that the boundaries of the zone were established when the agreement for the demilitarisation of the zone was signed? And that's important to establish for the purposes of this case.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could very well be, but for the sake of a criminal investigation about the facts that happened after the take-over, fixing the limits of the enclave was very far away from what I thought my duty was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer. Do you know that there existed a map of the demilitarised zone, or was there not such a map? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have not a clue about this since this demilitarised zone was created before the events I was tasked to investigate.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Since in your capacity as an investigator you investigated everything, do you know that the agreement on the demilitarised zone contained a map, and do you know where this map can be found today, and have you seen the map at all?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I have to repeat that the investigation - and this is what I always used to say - the investigation starts 11 July beginning of the afternoon after an air-raid that made everyone realise that the enclave would not be defended and people started to take to direction for fleeing, and subsequently you saw the number that I unfolded during my testimony happened. The investigation is about these events. I never looked into what could have happened in this area since 1992 and specially not into all the type of agreements that had been made regarding sharing of terrain or whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us, as an investigator, whether an ICTY investigator should keep in mind the agreement signed between two sides in an area that is the subject of a case before a court of law?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: My answer is no. The purpose of the investigation I was busy with was to identify what became the fate of both the civilians of that area and the military of that area once they ended up captured and in the custody of the Bosnian Serb army. That was the sole purpose of this investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you at all interested in what prompted the conflict and the events discussed in this case? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. My objective was not to try to explain why the perpetrators committed their acts but to prove the facts of the acts that they have committed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it at all important for this case, in accordance with the indictment which you should be aware of since you wrote it based on the information from your investigation, to know the genesis of the conflicts and problems that existed in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection to a misstatement of the fact. There's no indication that Mr. Ruez wrote any indictment, and so he needs to be careful not to misstate key facts. I will try to remain quiet, but key facts, like who wrote the indictment, I think I need to object to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, watch the objection of Mr. McCloskey. I'm quite sure that this witness was not the author of the indictment. Please carry on, but bear that in mind.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I am mindful of that, and I said in the latter part of my question that the indictment was written based on the information provided by Mr. Ruez as an investigator. I apologise if I erred or was -- went beyond the rules in my question. Thank you, Mr. President, I will bear that in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Ruez, based on what information did you draw the limits or boundaries of the enclave, and why did you draw them if they are not important? Or alternatively, what was the basis for the boundaries that you drew if you did not have direct information about it available? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is of so little importance for this investigation that what I drew on this map is the blue square that indicates the location of the Srebrenica safe area. This map is based on, if I remember well, a Dutch map. I don't exactly remember what we used as a background picture, but, again, had this map no observation posts and no grey zone as a boundary, my blue square would be far enough for the sake of what I wanted to explain to this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ruez. Can you mark for us on this map the urban area of Srebrenica. If you can, I would kindly ask you to mark it, if you can use this map. Otherwise we can call up a different map.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've left my glasses in the witness room, but I can succeed doing it without it. So roughly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The Court Officer will bring it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. But, I mean, roughly, anyhow, it's rough, this will be more or less the urban area of Srebrenica town.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Ruez.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I kindly ask the Presiding Judge to admit this map into evidence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit D19, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Ruez, yesterday at page 6 of the transcript you mentioned the gathering of the 28th Division in the area of the village of Susnjari. You did not pronounce it that way, but that's what you meant. Was it known how -- what the strength of the column was?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The total number of the column, the global assessment from various sources, puts the figure up to approximately 15.000 people among which, according to the information that I could receive from the 2nd Corps of the BiH Army, was that 6.000 men from the 28th Division arrived safely on Muslim-held territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us more precisely what the strength of the column was when it set out from Susnjari? That's what I meant. I didn't want to know how many of them arrived in Zenica [as interpreted]. But do you know what Ramiz --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't catch the last name.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: -- and other Muslim commanders said in terms of the column? I know that they mentioned women as well.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I have to say that the military historical part of this case was not the topic of the investigation. The investigation is about the fate of those who surrendered or were captured and ended up being prisoners of war in the hands of the Bosnian Serb army. I had no interest into looking if these people were carrying handguns, hunting guns, or heavy machine-guns, or tanks, or whatsoever. This was not the topic. The investigation is upon the fate of people who were -- ended up missing and who were captured prisoners. This is the topic of the investigation, not the military aspect of the surrounding battles or military aspects.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ruez. My question wasn't concerned with the weapons that they had. I only wanted to know the number of those who left, the number of those who managed to get out. So I was interested in the number of people who left Susnjari in the column. I suppose that you gained that information through your investigation and through the statements of individuals, some of whom appeared as witnesses here. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I already have answered this question. It was three questions before. You have the answer in the transcript. 15.000, among which 6.000 from the BiH Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us what of the remainder, if we subtract 6- from 15.000 we are left with a large number of people. What became of them? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: What became of them is exactly the topic of what my task was, since the number of the disappeared people was fixed by the ICRC at approximately 8.000. So the purpose of all this investigation was to determine where did these 8.000 vanish and what happened to them. This is exactly the heart of the investigation indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. There is a difference of 9.000 individuals. If 15.000 set out and only 6.000 managed to get out, according to your calculation 9.000 are missing. So the question remains what of these people, what happened to them?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: You misunderstood and you misread my answer, General. I said the column was composed of 15.000 people, among which 6.000 declared as being BiH Army personnel. So you have a difference of 9.000. Again, this number is an approximate. The number we rely on talking about missing persons is ICRC, 8.000.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I do agree that you should correct me if I misunderstand you. Just answer this question for me, will you: Do you know how many people set out from Susnjari and how many got out and reached Tuzla of the individuals belonging to that column? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection. This has been asked and answered several times now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President, but I would really want those who understand how many got out. If 15.000 set out and 6.000 were members of the army, what of these remaining 9.000? What are they? Civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can the witness answer that? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I really want to please you, I will say that one could consider that none of them was a civilian except the women since a few days before the enclave was taken over, there was an order of general mobilisation of all the men within the enclave. So, again, I have to insist that the sake of the investigation is to determine the fate of people who were prisoners, who ended up being prisoners. Either they were military dressed in military or military dressed in civilian clothes or total civilians, doesn't matter once their status is the one of the status of prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I understand. So in addition to women, there were 15.000 able-bodied men who set out, according to your investigation. Is my understanding correct?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: We can say it like this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did only 6.000 manage to get out or some of those who had been mobilised before they set out with the column? And I mean aside the 6.000 who were registered as members of the army, were there others who managed to get out? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, the goal of the investigation was not to determine how many people managed to get out alive of the Srebrenica safe area, but to determine the fate of those who were declared missing. So knowing how many people ended up alive in the area of Tuzla was really not the concern of this investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Based on your answer you have just provided, may I conclude that as a result of your investigation you basically did not learn of the exact number of those out of the column who eventually reached Tuzla? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, the precise number is not -- is not known to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ruez. I'm content with this answer. Yesterday in your testimony at page 8 of the transcript, line 21, you discussed a number of people assembled in Potocari. And without going into the figures, because I want you to share that information, what was the number of people who gathered there, in your view?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no precise figure. There were -- there were approximately 25.000 refugees coming from Srebrenica who arrived in Tuzla and the area of Tuzla and were in refugee camps. So to have a more precise figure of this number, I think the Red Cross could be the good source of information.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ruez. I pointed it out because yesterday at page 8, line 21, you stated that you tried to ascertain the number of those assembled in Potocari; that is the way I understood it. How did you as the investigator decide on the figure? Perhaps this may be of interest to the Chamber as well. And, please, bear with me for asking questions about things I don't know. I believe such pieces of information may be useful for both me and the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. Again, I have to insist on the fact that for the sake of the investigation the only number of importance is the number of people missing, since we hope at the end of the entire exhumation process and identification by DNA to have a very precise number of people that we can prove had been executed as they were prisoners. This is the important figure. For the other figures, the estimates, the estimates that everyone was using at that time was indeed a column of a strength of approximately 15.000 and a population of refugees of approximately 25.000. So that puts the total of the population inside the enclave to approximately 30.000, which was also an estimate of NGOs and UN and so on. But all these figures are estimates anyhow. I don't think anyone knows precisely what these numbers were.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Since you consulted various sources in your investigation as well as interviewed a number of witnesses who appeared in this case, can you tell us where this Defence can find the exact number of people who left Potocari and eventually set out for Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe the intelligence service of former Bosnian Serb army, they might have indications on this from their security offices and their personal sources.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. That was probably one of the channels you used yourself in your investigation. Since I have no means of contacting them, I wanted to ask you this: Do you know how many B&H soldiers set out from Srebrenica to Zepa?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I have to correct you. My sources, unfortunately, were not the security officers nor their commanders, talking about the intelligence service of Bosnian Serb army. I didn't say the BiH Army; I said the Bosnian Serb army. Regarding the second part of your question, indeed the number of 6.000 Bosnian -- BiH soldiers who reached safe territory, this figure was given to me by officers from the 2nd Corps of the BiH Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I am content with this answer. I noticed that you previously said that 6.000 soldiers arrived, but I was interested in the number of people who left Srebrenica and went towards Zepa. Can you please answer that.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: My task was the investigation on the events that follow the take-over of the Srebrenica safe area. I was at no point involved in the investigation regarding what happened after the fall of Zepa nor the military situation in between the Srebrenica situation and the Zepa situation. So I cannot answer your question, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I asked you this because the Prosecutor, when they put you on their witness list, stated that you were to testify on all relevant counts on the indictment. My indictment, as you know, includes Zepa. So the way I understand your answer is that you did not investigate Zepa as can be concluded based on your testimony. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: As an investigator and a person who interviewed a number of people appearing in this case, can you tell us how many people from Srebrenica eventually arrived in Zepa? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know only about one, because he is a survivor from the Kravica warehouse who then went to Zepa. In Zepa he was captured. He was put in a prison camp. And he was subsequently released, I think, among the last ones around February/March 1996. This is the only case of someone who had a connection with Zepa. I cannot say anything about Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: If possible, could you tell us the name of that person so that this Defence could rely on that source of information as well, or should we submit that request to the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you will have to request the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can we go into private session briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are now in public session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. McCloskey. We have received his name. We, nevertheless, wanted to ask the witness that, although we received that information from you. Among other things, we believe it is important to know how many people actually went to Zepa. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Witness, can you tell us why your investigation did not encompass Zepa and the events in that enclave, because it was included in both the Popovic et al. indictment as well as in my indictment? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The reason is simple. First, I do not decide as an investigator or even an investigation team leader what the topics of the investigation should be. I was busy with the events following the take-over of Srebrenica safe area. It was a task large enough, I think. And I have never been tasked to investigate events in Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ruez. First I'd like to clarify something before putting my question. Concerning certain portions of the Petrovic footage, you say that you learned of some of it as late as 2001. You said so yourself at page 10, lines 22 to 25. If I'm not mistaken, between -- since April 2001, you were no longer and investigator on the Srebrenica team and you did not work for The Hague Tribunal. How did you learn of this video under such circumstances? If you wish to refer to the exact part of your testimony, I would direct you to page 10, lines 22 to 25. How did you obtain that footage?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed, at that time, I was no longer a member of the OTP. I was on an island in the Caribs, and two journalists made the trip to show me the footages at my house. And that happened more or less in the same time-frame these footages had reached this Tribunal also.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ruez. After April 2001 after you stopped working for the Prosecutor's Office, did you take any part in any further Srebrenica investigations? Can you explain to us what you did between 2001 and later on? And in one of my following questions I will address the earlier period between 1995 and 2000.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: After April 2001, I did not continue at all working on the investigation, since I was no longer a member of this Tribunal. But I continued to be in contact with the Tribunal since I was supposed to continue to testify for whatever coming trial connected with this Srebrenica case.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: That you, Mr. Ruez. If this is so, after 2001 did you ever visit Srebrenica again? And if so, when and why?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: To Srebrenica as a precise location, yes. One was for the sake of the outreach programme of the Tribunal to give a conference in Srebrenica itself. And the other time was to accompany a journalist who wanted to do a report on the Srebrenica events. So twice to Srebrenica town.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: If it is not a secret, could you tell us what were the years? What was the year you went back for the first time and then the second?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: We reverse the thing, the first time was with the journalist; I think it was in 2002. I'm not a hundred per cent sure. And for outreach I'm not sure also; it might have been 2004, maybe 2005. I'm not certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. At the outreach conference, did any of the current OTP employees take part who had worked with you while you were a member of the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mark Harmon; senior trial attorney Mark Harmon was present in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ruez. In the course of today and yesterday in your testimony, you frequently mentioned witness statements. Did you have in mind the statements of witnesses given to you who -- or to the ICTY, and were these people soldiers or ex-B&H policemen? I am not sure whether I understood your testimony properly.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I always need to refer to witness statements because without these witness -- most of the goal of such an investigation is -- once you have compiled witness testimonies, is to create a chronology of events that enables you to have a view of a situation; and since you cannot buy the information provided as being facts, you then need to go on the ground and check the elements that can either implement what you heard from these people or what you read from their testimonies, or maybe also find out that due to what you can see on the ground these people have no credibility. So I always refer to witness testimonies; either people I interviewed myself, or people who were interviewed by other investigators. But it's a constant reference, indeed, to witness statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In order to have a complete answer, I would like to ask you this as well: Did you make use of the statements of those people whom you chose to have appear as witnesses, and did you provide their statements to B&H authorities and the MUP?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It went the way reverse. Once we had interviewed a witness, the sole destination of the information is the Prosecutor of the ICTY, never ever the local police or whoever in the area. Nevertheless, the way it worked the way around. Most of these witnesses, we found out about their existence by going through a huge number of statements that were initially collected by the Bosniak war crime commission and also by the MUP. And we went through all these statements in order to sort out among them those we believed were the most interesting. And then we systematically requested these people for an interview. We didn't take the counts given to the local police or the war crime commission, especially at the moment the events were very hot. So we re-interviewed, systematically, all those that we considered as being key information providers.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I asked you about this because there is a number of witnesses whose statements we received and were taken while you were the investigator, and there were also statements given to B&H authorities and the MUP. Such statements given to the B&H Army and MUP is something that these witnesses deemed as unimportant. That's why I wanted to ask you something about the method of selection of those witnesses and if you could please explain that.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As soon as July and August 1995, as we were in Tuzla during that summer, we got access to several hundreds of statements from the war crime commission that I already mentioned, from the MUP, from also -- some from UN civil affairs. We also spread questionnaires in refugee camps to NGOs in order for people who would have something of high relevance to be able to contact us. And based on all this, we made several packets, let's say. One packet was people who had information regarding the situation they experienced in Potocari. A second group was people who had things of importance to say about the deportation route between Potocari and Kladanj. And the main statements, those of utmost importance, was the last group of those who claimed having either witnessed executions or survived executions. And after that, the goal was to narrow down the information since for sure the survivors - there were not many - but interesting witnesses for all the rest, there were a lot, so we had to do a selection.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ruez.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, we are approaching the end of today's sitting. It's 5 minutes to 7.00. We learned that the Prosecution would like to raise some procedural matters. You will have plenty of time for your cross-examination, but for today I think we should break and end the cross-examination. I hope everybody can agree with that. Mr. Ruez, I think for today this concludes your examination and the cross-examination, but it's not the last day. You should -- Mr. Tolimir, you want to raise something?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Presiding Judge. I just wanted to thank Mr. Ruez, especially because we don't know when exactly he will continue his testimony. He provided specific and accurate answers to the questions I put. I just wanted to wish him a happy holidays when he rejoins his family. I would like to thank you again, Mr. Presiding judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Tolimir. Do you want to say something in the presence of the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, I think practically that would be a good idea. Mr. Ruez is used to being ordered not to speak to the Prosecution during the breaks in testimony. I've just realised I'm not aware of this Trial Chamber's practice in that regard. I don't think it's the law, frankly, I think it's a practice. So I would ask you that. But I would also -- there are two issues related to contacting him: One being the scheduling. Our next meetings are 14 and 15 April. We would like to get him in a two-day block which is as we all know we have, and we really need to be able to discuss with Mr. Ruez what days are the best for him. And I certainly hope that the General will finish in two days because it would be very difficult to bring Mr. Ruez back again for a third time. So if I will have a chance to discuss his best days. Ideally, the closer to now the better. But, as you know, we were hoping that without one of the witnesses we might be able to finish. This time, we didn't make it. But if I could speak to Mr. Ruez on logistic grounds and -- before he leaves, we should be able to get back to the Court the best day. So if it is, in fact, April 14th and 15th or perhaps the following week or the week after. So if I could have the ability to contact him on his schedule, we, of course, notified him that there's a good chance that he was coming back, so this is not a surprise, but we do need to connect with that so we can get the information for him and to you. The second is slightly less serious, but, nevertheless, important. We were hoping to be able to see Mr. Ruez tonight in a more social setting where we would, of course, not speak to him about the case at all but would - and I've informed Mr. Gajic of that fact - and would ask your requested approval for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Taking into account that you indicated 11 hours and 45 minutes for examination-in-chief and Mr. Tolimir indicated 10 hours of cross-examination, I think we can be optimistic that two days are enough for cross-examination, perhaps re-examination, and some additional questions by the Chamber. Dealing with the first problem. Mr. Ruez, could you indicate if you are available on the 14th and 15th of April?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is a bit too early for me to make sure of this. I first have to go back to my office and check a few things, but I think we can bet that I can come back before the end of April.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tolimir, you have heard about the wishes of the Prosecution to have the leave of the Chamber to contact him about scheduling of the continuing of your cross-examination. Are you in agreement with that?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Presiding Judge, the Defence trusts that both Mr. McCloskey and Mr. Ruez are professionals, having been in the trade for many years, and we do not want to pose any problems. We leave it in your hands to decide on the matter. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Do you have the same opinion for the second request, that Mr. McCloskey and colleagues are allowed to socialise with the witness for dinner or something like that if they promise not to raise any question to this case? Would you be in agreement with that?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. We are in agreement with that and do wish to enable them to meet and socialise as old friends either on private or professional business. We do not mind. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, your request is granted. You may contact the witness about the further appearance here in the Tribunal. And we wish you a wonderful Easter dinner together with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Are there any other questions about scheduling? No. Thank you very much. Mr. Ruez, for today you are free to return to your normal activities or for dinner, and we wish you and all others present in the courtroom happy Easter, good holidays, and all the best for you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We adjourn now, and resume on the 14th of April, 9.00, in this courtroom. We adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 14th day of April, 2010, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.04 p.m.,
